presentation.title: Doorstep Contractor / Home Repair Scam
presentation.summary: A person unexpectedly arrives at the door claiming to have noticed damage to the roof, driveway, gutters, or another part of the home. The person offers to make repairs immediately and claims the homeowner can receive a special discount by deciding today.
presentation.practiceGoal: Never agree to high-pressure home repairs without independent verification. Get a written estimate, verify the contractor's license and references, and seek a second opinion before paying a large deposit or allowing work to begin.

warningSigns.sign: An unsolicited contractor arrives at the home without being requested.
The contractor claims to have noticed serious damage that requires immediate repair.
The contractor offers a today-only discount or demands an immediate decision.
The contractor requests a large upfront cash deposit.
The contractor refuses to provide a written estimate, license information, or references.
The contractor uses fear or threats about the home being damaged to pressure the homeowner.

finalReview.safestAction: Do not agree to repairs or make a large payment during an unsolicited visit. End the conversation, verify the contractor independently, get a written estimate, and seek a second opinion from a trusted contractor.

realWorldActions.action: Do not allow an unexpected contractor to pressure you into making an immediate decision.
Ask for a written estimate describing the work, materials, total cost, and payment terms.
Verify the contractor's license, insurance, business information, and references independently.
Get a second opinion from a contractor you choose yourself.
Be cautious about large upfront cash deposits or requests for cash-only payment.
Do not let claims about dangerous or urgent damage prevent you from taking time to verify the situation.

artifact.heading: A contractor unexpectedly arrives at your door
artifact.message: The person says, "We're working nearby and noticed some damage on your roof. It looks like it needs immediate repair." The person offers to take a closer look and says they can explain the repair options.
artifact.transcript: A simulated contractor arrives unexpectedly at the learner's home. The contractor claims to have noticed damage and says the problem may require immediate attention. The contractor has not been independently verified.

scene.question: What would you do when an unexpected contractor arrives?
scene.description: An unsolicited contractor should not automatically be trusted simply because they claim to have noticed a problem with the home.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor was not invited or requested.
The contractor claims there is serious damage.
The contractor wants to discuss repairs immediately.

choice.title: Invite them inside to discuss the repair
choice.subtitle: Let the contractor inside so they can inspect the problem and explain the repair.

feedback.heading: An unexpected contractor should not be given immediate access
feedback.consequence: You allow an unverified person into your home before establishing who they are or whether the claimed damage actually exists.
feedback.explanation: Unsolicited home repair offers can involve pressure, exaggerated damage claims, or attempts to gain access to the property. You do not need to let an unexpected contractor inside.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor arrived without being requested.
The contractor has not provided independent proof of their identity or business.

choice.title: Speak through the door and ask for their business information
choice.subtitle: Keep the interaction outside and ask for the contractor's name and business information.

feedback.heading: You established a safer boundary
feedback.consequence: You avoid immediately giving an unexpected visitor access to your home.
feedback.explanation: Keeping the conversation outside gives you time to evaluate the situation. You can independently verify the contractor before considering any work.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor arrived unexpectedly.

choice.title: Say no and close the door
choice.subtitle: Decline the unsolicited repair offer and end the conversation.

feedback.heading: You avoided an unsolicited repair offer
feedback.consequence: You prevent the unexpected visitor from pressuring you into a repair decision.
feedback.explanation: You are not required to discuss home repairs with someone who unexpectedly arrives at your door. If you are concerned about the condition of your home, you can contact a contractor of your choice.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor initiated the contact unexpectedly.

artifact.heading: The contractor says the discount expires today
artifact.message: The contractor says, "I can do the work today for half price, but only if you decide right now. If I leave, I can't guarantee this price."
artifact.transcript: The simulated contractor offers a major discount but says the homeowner must make an immediate decision. The contractor has not provided a written estimate or allowed time for comparison with another contractor.

scene.question: What would you do when the contractor says the discount expires today?
scene.description: High-pressure deadlines are a warning sign. Legitimate contractors should allow time to review an estimate and compare options.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor creates an immediate deadline.
The contractor claims the price is available only today.
The contractor wants a decision before you can compare estimates.

choice.title: Agree because it sounds like a great deal
choice.subtitle: Accept the discounted price and let the contractor begin today.

feedback.heading: The discount was used to pressure you into acting quickly
feedback.consequence: You commit to a repair before independently verifying the contractor, the damage, or the actual cost of the work.
feedback.explanation: A large discount combined with an immediate deadline can be used to prevent you from comparing prices or checking the contractor's credentials.

warningSigns.sign: Today-only pricing.
Pressure to decide immediately.

choice.title: Ask for a written estimate and time to compare
choice.subtitle: Request the complete estimate in writing before making a decision.

feedback.heading: You slowed down the decision
feedback.consequence: You avoid being pressured into accepting a repair without documentation.
feedback.explanation: A written estimate should explain the work, materials, total cost, and payment terms. Taking time to compare estimates can help identify unreasonable prices or suspicious contractors.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor wanted an immediate decision.

choice.title: Ask a neighbor what they think
choice.subtitle: Ask someone nearby whether they know anything about the contractor.

feedback.heading: Outside advice can help, but it does not verify the contractor
feedback.consequence: You gain another perspective, but the contractor still has not been independently verified.
feedback.explanation: Trusted people can provide useful advice, but you should still verify the contractor's business information and obtain a written estimate before agreeing to work.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor is still pressuring you to make a decision.

artifact.heading: The contractor requests a {{depositAmount}} cash deposit
artifact.message: The contractor says, "I need {{depositAmount}} in cash right now for materials. Once you pay the deposit, I can get started today."
artifact.transcript: The simulated contractor requests a {{depositAmount}} cash deposit before work begins. The contractor has not provided enough documentation to independently establish the legitimacy of the business or the repair.

scene.question: What would you do when the contractor asks for a {{depositAmount}} cash deposit?
scene.description: A large upfront cash payment to an unverified contractor is a major warning sign. Do not pay until the contractor and agreement have been independently verified.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor requests a large upfront payment.
The payment must be made in cash.
The contractor wants payment before verification and before work begins.

choice.title: Pay the {{depositAmount}} cash deposit
choice.subtitle: Give the contractor the requested cash so the work can begin immediately.

feedback.heading: A large cash deposit creates a serious financial risk
feedback.consequence: You give {{depositAmount}} in cash to an unverified contractor. The contractor could take the payment and leave without completing the work.
feedback.explanation: Large cash deposits should not be made to an unsolicited contractor without verifying the business, reviewing a written agreement, and understanding the payment terms.

warningSigns.sign: Large upfront cash payment.
Unverified contractor.

choice.title: Offer a smaller partial payment
choice.subtitle: Offer to give the contractor a smaller amount of money to show good faith.

feedback.heading: A smaller payment is still risky without verification
feedback.consequence: You reduce the amount of money at risk, but you are still paying an unverified contractor.
feedback.explanation: Changing the amount does not solve the underlying problem. Verify the contractor and have a written agreement before making a payment.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor has not been independently verified.
The contractor is requesting money before the work begins.

choice.title: Refuse the cash deposit and verify the contractor
choice.subtitle: Do not pay until you verify the contractor, references, license, and written agreement.

feedback.heading: You protected yourself from an upfront-payment scam
feedback.consequence: You keep control of your money while you independently verify the contractor.
feedback.explanation: Do not let a contractor's payment deadline prevent you from checking the business and getting documentation. A legitimate contractor should be willing to discuss payment terms in writing.

warningSigns.sign: Large cash deposit request.
Pressure to pay immediately.

artifact.heading: The contractor uses fear to pressure you
artifact.message: The contractor becomes annoyed and says, "Your roof could collapse. I'm trying to help you. If you don't let me fix it today, the damage could get much worse."
artifact.transcript: The simulated contractor becomes increasingly urgent and claims that the homeowner could face serious damage if they do not agree to repairs immediately. The contractor uses fear to discourage the homeowner from seeking another opinion.

scene.question: What would you do when the contractor pressures you with a scary warning?
scene.description: Fear and urgency can make people act before they have time to verify a claim. Do not allow pressure to replace an independent inspection.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor claims the home is in immediate danger.
The contractor discourages you from waiting or getting another opinion.
The contractor uses fear to pressure you into agreeing to repairs.

choice.title: Give in to the pressure
choice.subtitle: Agree to the repair because you are worried the home could be damaged.

feedback.heading: Fear caused you to bypass verification
feedback.consequence: You allow the contractor's warning to determine your decision before independently confirming that the claimed damage exists.
feedback.explanation: Scammers may exaggerate or invent problems to create fear. Even if a repair really is needed, you can choose a contractor and verify the problem yourself.

warningSigns.sign: Fear-based pressure.
Immediate repair demand.

choice.title: End the conversation and call a trusted contractor
choice.subtitle: Ask the visitor to leave and contact a contractor you choose yourself.

feedback.heading: You took control of the decision
feedback.consequence: You stop the pressure and create an opportunity to independently inspect and verify the claimed problem.
feedback.explanation: A trusted contractor can inspect the property and provide an independent opinion. The person who arrives unexpectedly should not control the repair decision.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor used fear to demand immediate action.

choice.title: Ask them to come back tomorrow
choice.subtitle: Delay the decision and tell the contractor you will think about it.

feedback.heading: Delaying helps, but independent verification is still needed
feedback.consequence: You create time to think, but the same contractor may return and continue the pressure.
feedback.explanation: Waiting is safer than making an immediate decision, but you should still verify the contractor independently and get another opinion before agreeing to work.

warningSigns.sign: The contractor is using urgency to control the decision.

artifact.heading: Pause before paying for unexpected home repairs
artifact.message: Unsolicited contractors, today-only discounts, large cash deposits, missing paperwork, and fear-based pressure are warning signs. You do not have to make an immediate repair decision.
artifact.transcript: The guide reminds the learner that unexpected home repair offers should be treated carefully. A contractor who arrives without being requested may use urgency, discounts, large upfront payments, or fear about property damage to pressure the homeowner. The safest approach is to slow down, get a written estimate, verify the contractor, and seek a second opinion.

scene.question: What is the safest response to an unexpected home repair offer?
scene.description: Do not allow an unexpected contractor to pressure you into repairs or payment. Verify the contractor and the claimed damage independently.

warningSigns.sign: Unsolicited contractor
Today-only discount
Large upfront cash deposit
No written estimate or contract
No license or references
Pressure and fear about immediate damage

choice.title: Verify the contractor and get a second opinion
choice.subtitle: Get a written estimate, independently verify the contractor, and compare another opinion before paying.

feedback.heading: Excellent
feedback.consequence: You recognized the warning signs and avoided making a pressured repair decision.
feedback.explanation: The safest approach is to slow down. Get the proposed work and price in writing, verify the contractor using information you find independently, and ask another trusted contractor to inspect the problem.

warningSigns.sign: Unsolicited repair offers should be independently verified.
High-pressure payment demands are a warning sign.

artifact.heading: Safe verification completed
artifact.message: The contractor was declined or independently verified before any commitments were made.
artifact.transcript: The learner successfully avoided the unsolicited offer, declined upfront cash, or independently verified the contractor and estimates.

outcome.label: Contractor verified safely
outcome.heading: You avoided high-pressure repairs
outcome.explanation: You protected your home and finances by refusing unsolicited visits and demanding proper documentation and independent verification.

warningSigns.sign: Unsolicited contractor arrival.
High-pressure tactics and urgency.
